title: Commentarius in Ecclesiasten
author: Incertus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp436.tmp436.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: » Cum superioribus autem congruit, quod nihil no- vum in mundo fiat : nec sit aliquis 7, qui possit exsistere, et dicere, ecce hoc novum est : siquidem omne quod se putaverit novum ostendere, jam in prioribus saeculis fuit. Nec putemus signa, atque prodigia, et multa, quae arbitrio Dei nova in inundo fiunt, in prioribus saeculis esse jam facta; et lo- cum invenire Epicurum, qui asserit per innumera- biles periodos eadem, et eisdem in locis, et per eosdem fieri. Alioquin et Judas crebro prodidit, et Christus passus est saepe pro nobis, et cartera quae facta sunt, et futura, in easdem similiter periodos revolventur.
passages.english: Now it agrees with what precedes that nothing new comes about in the world, and that there is no one who could stand up and say, "Look, this is new," since everything that he thinks he is showing to be new already existed in earlier ages. Yet we should not suppose that the signs and wonders, and the many things that come about new in the world by the will of God, were already done in earlier ages, and so give room to Epicurus, who asserts that the same things happen through countless cycles, in the same places and through the same persons. Otherwise Judas too has betrayed many times, and Christ has suffered for us often, and everything else that has been done and will be done will likewise come round again in the same cycles.
passages.notes: The figure "7" after "aliquis" is a footnote mark and has been omitted. "inundo" is read as "mundo" and "cartera" as "caetera". Assigning the doctrine of recurring cycles to Epicurus is the text's own attribution.

passages.original: In multitudine enim bonorum multi sunt, qui comedunt ea 9, et quae est fortitudo habenti illa, nisi ut videat oculis suis? Ubicunque argentum ponimus, secundum Graeci sermonis ambiguitatem, potest et pecunia transferri : άργΰριον quippe utrumque significat. Porro Tullius pecuniosos pri- mitus eos dictos refert, qui plura habuissent pe- culia 1, id est pecora. Ita enim ea antiquitus ap- pellabant. Paulatim autem per abusionem, nomen ad aliud devolutum est. Avarus igitur describitur, quod nunquam opibus expleatur, et quanto plus habuerit, tanto plus cupiat.
passages.english: For where goods abound, many are those who eat them; and what strength does the one who has them have, except that he sees [them] with his eyes? Wherever we put "silver," it can also be rendered "money," following the ambiguity of the Greek word, for argyrion means both. Further, Tullius records that those were first called pecuniosi ("moneyed") who had more peculia, that is, cattle, for that is what they called them in ancient times. Gradually, however, through misuse, the name passed over to something else. So the miser is described, in that he is never filled with wealth, and the more he has, the more he desires.
passages.notes: The figures "9" and "1" are footnote marks and have been omitted. "Tullius" is Cicero. The first sentence is the lemma from Ecclesiastes 5:10. The text reads "fortitudo" (strength); the usual Vulgate reading is a different word meaning "profit", so the sense of this word here is uncertain.

passages.original: Et cum sint plurimi, qui Scripturarum occulta dicant posse se solvere 9, rarus est, qui veram inveniat solutionem. Quod au- tem sequitur : Sapientia hominis illuminabit vul- tum ejus, et improbus facie eoa odietur, » ita pos- sumus explanare, ut Pauli verba ponamus : Nos autem omnes revelata facie gloriam Domini contem- plantes (II Cor. III, 18); et Psalmistae canentis : Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui. Domine (Psal.IV, 7). Sapientiam autem hic hominis non aliam dicit absque sapientia Dei. Quae cum sapten- tia Dei sit, juxta possibilitatem capacitatis hominis ejus esse incipit, qui se habere meruerit. Omnis haereticus et falsum dogma defendens, impudenti vultu est. Denique Marcion et Valentinus 10 melioris se dicunt naturae esse, quam conditor est. Et hoc posset aliqua ex parte ferri, si spem se hujus rei habere contenderent, et non jam possidere naturam.
passages.english: And although there are very many who say that they can solve the hidden things of the Scriptures, rare is the one who finds the true solution. What follows, "The wisdom of a man will illuminate his face, and the shameless one will be hated for his face," we can explain by setting beside it the words of Paul: "But we all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face" (2 Cor. 3:18); and of the Psalmist, who sings: "The light of your countenance has been sealed upon us, Lord" (Ps. 4:7). Here he calls the wisdom of man none other than the wisdom of God. Though it is the wisdom of God, it begins to belong, according to the measure of a man's capacity, to the one who has deserved to have it. Every heretic, and everyone defending a false doctrine, is of shameless face. Indeed, Marcion and Valentinus say that they are of a better nature than the Creator is. And this could be tolerated in some measure if they claimed to have hope of this thing, and not to possess that nature already.
passages.notes: "facie eoa" is read as "facie sua" (scanning error); "saptentia" read as "sapientia". Stray numerals (9, 10) are footnote marks and have been omitted.

passages.original: Neque enim frivola debes formidare commenta, quod singulorum operum, vel bonorum vel malorum, apud inferos tibi reddenda sit [Al. est] ratio. Non est enim aliqua in morte sapientia : nullus post dissolu- tionem vitae hujus remanet 5 sensus. Et haec, inquit, aliquis loquatur Epicurus 6, et Aristippus et Cyre- naici, et caeterae pecudes philosophorum. Ego autem mecum diligenter retractans, invenio non, ut quidam male aestimant, omnia fortuito geri, et variam in rebus humanis fortunam ludere, sed cuncta judicio Dei fieri.
passages.english: For you need not fear the trivial fictions that an account must be rendered to you in the underworld for each of your deeds, whether good or bad. For there is no wisdom in death; no awareness remains after the dissolution of this life. "And let some Epicurus say these things," he says, "and Aristippus and the Cyrenaics and the other cattle among the philosophers. But I, carefully going over it in my own mind, find not, as some wrongly suppose, that all things are done by chance and that a fickle fortune plays in human affairs, but that all things come about by the judgement of God."
passages.notes: The figures "5" and "6" are footnote marks and have been omitted. [Al. est] is a variant reading noted by the edition ("est" for "sit"); it does not change the sense. The opening sentences continue the speech of the hedonist that the commentator voices before refuting it. The exact limits of the quotation introduced by "inquit" are uncertain.
